topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Initial measurement of PPE at cost - directly attributable costs and decommissioning/restoration estimate included, initial operating losses excluded
question_html:
Preet Ltd. is installing a new plant at its production facility. It has incurred these costs:

Particulars₹
Cost of the plant (cost per supplier's invoice plus taxes)10,00,000
Initial delivery and handling costs80,000
Cost of site preparation2,40,000
Consultants used for advice on the acquisition of the plant2,80,000
Estimated dismantling costs to be incurred after 7 years1,20,000
Operating losses before commercial production1,60,000

Please advise Preet Ltd. on the costs that can be capitalised in accordance with AS 10 (Revised). (5 Marks)
answer_html:
According to AS 10 (Revised), these costs can be capitalised:

#Particulars₹
1.Cost of the plant10,00,000
2.Initial delivery and handling costs80,000
3.Cost of site preparation2,40,000
4.Consultants' fees2,80,000
5.Estimated dismantling costs to be incurred after 7 years1,20,000
Total17,20,000

Note: Operating losses before commercial production amounting to ₹1,60,000 are not regarded as directly attributable costs and thus cannot be capitalized. They should be written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period they are incurred.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is including the pre-commercial-production operating losses in the capitalised cost of the plant, on the mistaken reasoning that they were incurred before the asset was ready for use – AS 10 specifically excludes initial operating losses as a directly attributable cost, regardless of timing.

topic_text: Topic 2.5/2.6/2.9: Nil depreciation when residual value equals cost; freehold land not depreciated; depreciation on a self-constructed asset begins when ready for use, not when actually used; revised useful-life estimate spread prospectively over the remaining life
question_html:
A Ltd. had following assets. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2023 for each asset as per AS 10 (Revised):

  1. Machinery purchased for ₹10 lakhs on 1st April, 2018 and residual value after useful life of 5 years, based on 2018 prices is ₹10 lakhs.
  2. Land for ₹50 lakhs.
  3. A Machinery is constructed for ₹5,00,000 for its own use (useful life is 10 years). Construction is completed on 1st April, 2022, but the company does not begin using the machine until 31st March, 2023.
  4. Machinery purchased on 1st April, 2020 for ₹50,000 with useful life of 5 years and residual value is NIL. On 1st April, 2022, management decided to use this asset for further 2 years only. (4 Parts × 5 Marks = 20 Marks)
answer_html:
Computation of amount of depreciation as per AS 10

AssetDepreciation (₹)
(i) Machinery purchased on 1/4/18 for ₹10 lakhs (having residual value of ₹10 lakhs).
Reason: The company considers that the residual value, based on prices prevailing at the balance sheet date, will equal the cost. Therefore, there is no depreciable amount and depreciation is correctly zero.		Nil
(ii) Land (₹50 lakhs) (considered freehold).
Reason: Land has an unlimited useful life and therefore, it is not depreciated.		Nil
(iii) Machinery constructed for own use (₹5,00,000/10).
Reason: The entity should begin charging depreciation from the date the machine is ready for use i.e. 1st April, 2022. The fact that the machine was not used for a period after it was ready to be used is not relevant in considering when to begin charging depreciation.		50,000
(iv) Machinery having revised useful life.
Reason: The entity has charged depreciation using the straight-line method at ₹10,000 per annum i.e. (50,000/5 years). On 1st April, 2022 the asset’s net book value is [50,000 − (10,000 × 2)] i.e. ₹30,000. The remaining useful life is 2 years as per revised estimate. The company should amend the annual provision for depreciation to charge the unamortized cost over the revised remaining life of 2 years. Consequently, it should charge depreciation for the next 2 years at ₹15,000 per annum i.e. (30,000/2 years).		15,000
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error on part (iii) is deferring the start of depreciation to the date the machine is actually put into use rather than the date it becomes ready for use, and on part (iv) treating the revised remaining life as a fresh 5-year period instead of amending the existing straight-line rate to spread the asset's already-reduced net book value over only the 2 years actually remaining.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Costs excluded from PPE cost even though incidental to acquiring/renovating the asset - pre-opening staff costs and reorganisation-type expenditure not directly attributable to bringing the asset to its intended working condition are expensed, not capitalised
question_html:
Neon Enterprise operates a major chain of restaurants located in different cities. The company has acquired a new restaurant located at Chandigarh. The new-restaurant requires significant renovation expenditure. Management expects that the renovations will last for 3 months during which the restaurant will be closed.

Management has prepared the following budget for this period –

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Salaries of the staff engaged in preparation of restaurant before its opening7,50,000
Construction and remodelling cost of restaurant30,00,000

Explain the treatment of these expenditures as per the provisions of AS 10 "Property, Plant and Equipment".
answer_html: Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of reducing or reorganizing the operations of the company. These costs do not meet that requirement of AS 10 “Property, Plant and Equipment” and cannot, therefore, be capitalized.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the pre-opening staff salaries and the construction/remodelling cost identically merely because both fall within the same closure period, without separately testing each item against AS 10's directly-attributable-cost condition.

topic_text: Topic 2.9: PPE acquired in exchange for a non-monetary asset, combined with WDV-method depreciation across an acquisition/disposal/exchange within the year
question_html:
In the books of Topmaker Limited, carrying amount of Plant and Machinery as on 1st April, 2022 is ₹56,30,000.

On scrutiny, it was found that a purchase of Machinery worth ₹21,12,000 was included in the purchase of goods on 1st June, 2022. On 30th June, 2022 the company disposed a Machine having book value of ₹9,60,000 (as on 1st April, 2022) for ₹8,25,000 in part exchange of a new machine costing ₹15,65,000.

The company charges depreciation @ 10% p.a. on written down value method on Plant and Machinery.

You are required to compute: (i) Depreciation to be charged to Profit & Loss Account; (ii) Book value of Plant & Machinery as on 31st March, 2023; and (iii) Profit/Loss on exchange of Plant & Machinery. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Depreciation to be charged in the Profit & Loss Account

ParticularsAmount in ₹
Depreciation on old Machinery [10% on ₹56,30,000 for 3 months (01.04.2022 to 30.06.2022)]1,40,750
Add: Depreciation on Machinery acquired on 01.06.2022 (₹21,12,000 × 10% × 10/12)1,76,000
Add: Depreciation on Machinery after adjustment of Exchange [10% of (₹56,30,000 − 9,60,000 + 15,65,000) for 9 months]4,67,625
Total Depreciation to be charged in Profit & Loss A/c7,84,375

(ii) Book value of Plant & Machinery as on 31.3.2023

ParticularsAmount in ₹
Balance as per books on 01.04.202256,30,000
Add: Included in purchases on 01.06.202221,12,000
Add: Purchases on 30.06.202215,65,00036,77,000
(subtotal)93,07,000
Less: Book value of Machine sold on 30.06.2022(9,60,000)
(subtotal)83,47,000

Book Value as on 31.03.202375,86,625

Note: the computation of depreciation and book value of Plant & Machinery can be presented in the following alternative manner:

ParticularsBook Value or Cost or AcquisitionPeriodDepreciationBook Value as on 31.03.2023
Opening Value46,70,000 (56,30,000 − 9,60,000)01.04.2022 to 31.03.20234,67,000 (46,70,000 × 10%)42,03,000
Sold9,60,00001.04.2022 to 30.06.202224,000 (9,60,000 × 10% × 3/12)–

New Machinery15,65,00001.07.2022 to 31.03.20231,17,375 (15,65,000 × 10% × 9/12)14,47,625
Total7,84,37575,86,625

(iii) Profit/Loss on Exchange of Machinery

ParticularsAmount in ₹
Balance as per books on 01.04.20229,60,000
Less: Depreciation for 3 months (₹9,60,000 × 10/100 × 3/12)(24,000)
W.D.V. as on 30.06.20229,36,000
Less: Exchange value(8,25,000)

mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees computed depreciation for the exchanged machine only up to the date of disposal without also computing a full 9-month depreciation charge on the new machine's cost from the date of exchange, understating the year's total depreciation figure. Some examinees also used the exchange value (₹8,25,000) directly as the sale proceeds without first reducing the old machine's book value to its 30th June written-down value, misstating the loss transferred on exchange.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Costs of relocating/reorganising operations excluded from the cost of an asset; computing the directly attributable acquisition cost of land net of recoverable GST on salvage proceeds
question_html:
Hardy Ltd. intends to extend the factory set up on the adjacent plot with disintegrated old premises. It acquired the land having an area of 250 hectares at a cost of ₹25,000 per hectare.

Hardy Ltd. incurred Stamp duty and registration charges of 5% of land value. Legal fees were paid ₹4,75,000 for land acquisition.

Hardy Ltd. incurred ₹37,85,000 for demolishing old premises thereon. A sum of ₹12,60,000 (including 5% GST thereon) was realized from the sale of material salvaged from the site.

Till the new site with extended factory premises is ready, the company needs to move the present production facilities to another (temporary) site. The following incremental costs will be incurred.

(1) Set up costs of ₹7,50,000 to install machinery in the new location. (2) Rent of ₹12,00,000. (3) Removal costs of ₹2,50,000 to transport the machinery from the old location to the temporary location.

(i) Management is of the opinion that the cost of moving the production facilities to another temporary location can be capitalised. You are required to advise. (ii) You are also required to compute the cost of land acquired. (7 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of relocating or reorganising operations of the company and do not meet the requirement of AS 10 (Revised). Therefore, these costs cannot be capitalized.

(ii) Computation of cost of land:

Particulars₹
Purchase Price250 hectares × ₹25,000 per hectare62,50,000
Stamp Duty and Registration Charges5% of ₹62,50,0003,12,500
Legal and Consultancy Fees4,75,000
Demolition Expenses (Net of Salvage Income)₹37,85,000 − ₹12,60,000 × (100/105) [i.e. ₹37,85,000 − ₹12,00,000]25,85,000
Cost of Land96,22,500
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: A significant number of examinees displayed a lack of understanding of the provisions of AS 10 "Property, Plant and Equipment." Instead of applying the correct provisions, many examinees incorrectly based their responses on AS 16 — Borrowing Costs, especially while commenting on the capitalisation of expenses related to the relocation of production facilities. Additionally, several examinees were unable to accurately compute the cost of land.

topic_text: Topic 2.10: Replacement of a significant component: capitalise the new part's cost and derecognise the estimated carrying amount of the part replaced
question_html:
MS Ltd. has acquired a heavy machinery at a cost of ₹1,00,00,000 (with no breakdown of the component parts). The estimated useful life is 10 years. At the end of the sixth year, one of the major components, the turbine requires replacement, as further maintenance is uneconomical. The remainder of the machine is perfect and is expected to last for the next four years. The cost of a new turbine is ₹45,00,000. The discount rate assumed is 5%.

Can the cost of the new turbine be recognised as an asset, and, if so, what treatment should be used?
answer_html:
The new turbine will produce economic benefits to MS Ltd., and the cost is measurable. Hence, the item should be recognised as an asset. The original invoice for the machine did not specify the cost of the turbine; however, the cost of the replacement ₹45,00,000 can be used as an indication (usually by discounting) of the likely cost, six years previously.

Statement showing cost of new turbine and machine after 6th year

Cost of machine recognized on purchase1,00,00,000
Less: Depreciation charged for 6 years [(1,00,00,000/10) × 6](60,00,000)
40,00,000
Less: Current cost of turbine to be derecognized:
Cost of Turbine before 6 years [45,00,000 × {1/(1.05)6}]33,57,900
Less: Depreciation for 6 years [(33,57,900/10) × 6](20,14,740)(13,43,160)
Add: Cost of new turbine to be recognised45,00,000
Revised carrying amount of machine71,56,840
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is expensing the replacement turbine's cost entirely, or recognising it without first derecognising the estimated carrying amount of the original turbine component being replaced, resulting in double-counting of the turbine's net book value under AS 10's component approach.

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Nil depreciable amount when residual value equals cost
question_html: Machinery purchased 1st April, 2020 for ₹10 lakhs, useful life 5 years, residual value (at 2020 prices) ₹10 lakhs. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025 per AS 10 (Revised).
answer_html: Nil. Since the residual value (₹10 lakhs) equals the cost (₹10 lakhs), the depreciable amount is nil; depreciation is correctly zero throughout the asset's life.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees computed depreciation on the full cost, ignoring the stated residual value entirely.

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Freehold land is not depreciated - unlimited useful life
question_html: The company owns a piece of land acquired for ₹50 lakhs, held for use in its factory operations. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: Nil. Land has an unlimited useful life (unless it is a wasting asset such as a quarry) and is therefore not depreciated.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A basic but recurring error is depreciating land alongside buildings without separating the two components.

topic_text: Topic 2.6: Depreciation begins when the asset is ready for use, not when actual use commences
question_html: Zenith Ltd. constructed a machine for its own use, total cost ₹5,00,000, completed 1st April, 2024, useful life 10 years; the company did not commence using the machine until 31st March, 2025. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: ₹50,000 (₹5,00,000/10 years). Depreciation begins from the date the machine is ready for use (1st April, 2024), regardless of when actual use commenced — the fact that it sat idle for a period after being ready is not relevant to when depreciation begins.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees charged no depreciation at all, reasoning the machine was never actually used during the year, missing that "ready for use" (not actual use) triggers depreciation.

topic_text: Topic 2.9: Revised useful-life estimate - unamortised cost spread prospectively over the revised remaining life
question_html: Another machine was purchased 1st April, 2022, for ₹50,000, useful life 5 years, nil residual value. On 1st April, 2024, management decided the machine would now be used for only two more years. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: Original SLM depreciation = ₹50,000/5 = ₹10,000/year. Net book value on 1st April, 2024 (after 2 years) = 50,000−20,000 = ₹30,000. With the revised remaining useful life of 2 years, the unamortised cost is spread over the revised remaining life: 30,000/2 = ₹15,000/year for the next 2 years.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees continued the original ₹10,000/year rate, not recognising that a revised useful-life estimate requires recomputing the annual charge over the remaining life going forward.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Cost of a PPE item as purchase price plus directly attributable costs, at actual cost with internal profit eliminated
question_html:
Shrishti Ltd. contracted with a supplier to purchase machinery which is to be installed in its Department A in three months' time. Special foundations were required for the machinery which were to be prepared within this supply lead time. The cost of the site preparation and laying foundations were ₹1,41,870. These activities were supervised by a technician during the entire period, who is employed for this purpose at ₹45,000 per month. The technician's services were given by Department B to Department A, which billed the services at ₹49,500 per month after adding 10% profit margin.

The machine was purchased at ₹1,58,34,000 inclusive of IGST @ 12% for which input credit is available to Shrishti Ltd. ₹55,770 transportation charges were incurred to bring the machine to the factory site. An Architect was appointed at a fee of ₹30,000 to supervise machinery installation at the factory site.

Ascertain the amount at which the Machinery should be capitalized under AS 10, considering that IGST credit is availed by Shrishti Limited. Internally booked profits should be eliminated in arriving at the cost of machine.
answer_html:
ParticularsBasis₹
Purchase PriceGiven (₹1,58,34,000 × 100/112, IGST credit removed)1,41,37,500
Add: Site Preparation CostGiven1,41,870
Add: Technician's SalarySpecific/attributable overhead for 3 months, at cost, no internal profit (45,000 × 3)1,35,000
Add: Transportation ChargesInitial delivery cost, given55,770
Add: Architect's FeesProfessional fees for installation, given30,000
Total Cost of Asset1,45,00,140

The technician's cost is included at its actual salary cost of ₹45,000/month (attributable overhead directly related to bringing the asset to its working condition), not the ₹49,500/month inter-departmental billing rate, since the 10% mark-up billed by Department B to Department A is an internally booked profit that must be eliminated when arriving at the cost of the machine for external financial reporting.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising the technician's cost at the ₹49,500/month inter-departmental billing rate rather than the actual ₹45,000/month salary cost, failing to eliminate the internally booked 10% profit margin as the question explicitly requires.

topic_text: Topic 2.4: Directly attributable costs capitalised, including net trial-run/testing cost after deducting any proceeds from test output
question_html: Precision Tools Ltd. purchased a machine for ₹12,00,000 on 1st October 2024. Additional expenses: Freight and insurance ₹60,000; Erection charges ₹40,000; Testing cost — raw materials used ₹25,000, wages ₹10,000, sale of finished goods from testing production ₹8,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized for this machine per AS 10.
answer_html:
Purchase Price12,00,000
Freight & Insurance60,000
Erection Charges40,000
Net Cost of Testing (25,000+10,000−8,000 sale proceeds)27,000
Cost of Machinery13,27,000
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees capitalised the gross testing cost (35,000) without netting off the ₹8,000 proceeds from sale of test-run output.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Component replacement - derecognise the replaced component's carrying amount, capitalise the new component's cost
question_html: On 1st December 2024, Precision Tools Ltd. replaced the motor of an old machine with a new one costing ₹1,20,000, improving output capacity by 15%. The old motor had cost ₹50,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹35,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Carrying amount of the old motor = 50,000−35,000 = ₹15,000, which is derecognised (written off) since it is being replaced. The new motor's acquisition cost of ₹1,20,000 is capitalised as a separate component (component accounting under AS 10). Net effect: ₹1,20,000 capitalised, ₹15,000 carrying amount of the old motor removed/expensed.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees simply added the new motor's cost to the machine's carrying value without also derecognising the replaced motor's remaining carrying amount.

topic_text: Topic 2.4: Relocation/reorganisation costs are never capitalised, regardless of connection to a specific asset
question_html: On 15th March 2025, Precision Tools Ltd. shifted a machine from one factory to another, incurring: Dismantling cost ₹12,000; Transport and installation ₹18,000; Loss due to damage in transit ₹6,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Nil is capitalised — costs of relocating or reorganising part or all of an enterprise's operations are not included in the carrying amount of PPE under AS 10. The entire ₹36,000 (12,000+18,000+6,000) is charged off to the Profit and Loss Account.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees capitalised the transport and installation cost, reasoning it was directly attributable to the machine, missing AS 10's specific exclusion of relocation costs regardless of their connection to a particular asset.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Cost of installation - directly attributable labour/supervisor/testing costs; deferred-credit interest excluded   +   Topic 7.13/7.16: Impairment loss on a revalued asset - first set off against the revaluation reserve balance, remainder to P&L
question_html:
On 1 April, 2022, Sky Limited purchased a machinery for ₹7,35,000 (inclusive of GST @5%, input credit available for entire amount). Other installation expenses: Cost of preparation of site ₹16,500; Total Labour charges ₹75,000 (200 of 500 total men hours spent on installation); Total salary of supervisor ₹34,000 (25% of time spent on installation); Interest charges paid to supplier for deferred credit ₹8,000; Test run and experimental production expenses ₹28,200; Consultancy charges to architect for plant set up ₹18,800; Depreciation on assets used for installation ₹8,000. The machine was ready for use on October 1, 2022 but was put to use from February 1, 2023 (further expenses of ₹10,800 incurred due to this delay). Estimated useful life 10 years, SLM, no residual value.

On September 30, 2025, the company revalued the machine at ₹7 lakhs, surplus credited to revaluation reserve. For the year ended March 31, 2026, conditions indicating impairment existed and the recoverable amount was ascertained to be only ₹3 Lakhs.

You are required to: (i) Calculate the value at which the machine should be capitalized and the amount of depreciation to be charged for the year ending March 31, 2023 in the books of Sky Limited. (ii) Calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Sky Limited. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Calculation of Cost of Machinery:

Purchase Price7,35,000
Add: Site Preparation Cost16,500
Labour charges (75,000 × 200/500)30,000
Supervisor's Salary (25% of 34,000)8,500
Test run and experimental production charges28,200
Architect Fees for set up18,800
Depreciation on assets used for installation8,000
Total Cost of Asset8,45,000
Less: GST credit receivable(35,000)
Value to be capitalized8,10,000
Depreciation to be charged on 31.3.2023 (for 6 months, SLM 10 year)40,500

Note: (i) Further expenses of ₹10,800 from 1.10.2022 to 1.2.2023 are charged to profit and loss A/c, as the plant was ready for production on 1.10.2022 (already capitalised) – the delay in actual use does not extend capitalisation. (ii) Interest charges of ₹8,000 paid on deferred credit terms to the supplier of the plant (not a qualifying asset) are not directly attributable costs and are written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period incurred.

(ii) Statement showing impairment loss and its treatment:

Carrying amount of the machine as on 01/10/20228,10,000
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (8,10,000 x 3/10)(2,43,000)
Carrying amount as on 30/09/20255,67,000
Add: Upward revaluation (credited to revaluation reserve)1,33,000
Carrying amount of the machine as on 30/09/2025 (post-revaluation)7,00,000
Less: Depreciation for 6 months up to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7)(50,000)
Carrying amount as on 31/03/20266,50,000
Less: Recoverable amount(3,00,000)
Impairment Loss3,50,000
Less: balance in revaluation reserve as on 31/03/2026 [1,33,000 − (50,000−40,500)](1,23,500)
Impairment Loss to be debited to Profit & Loss Account2,26,500

Depreciation for 01/10/2025 to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹50,000. Depreciation set off against Revaluation Reserve = (1,33,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹9,500 (Impairment loss set off against revaluation reserve balance as per para 58 of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets").
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees debited the entire ₹3,50,000 impairment loss to the profit and loss account, not applying AS 28's requirement (para 58) to first set off an impairment loss on a revalued asset against the remaining balance in that asset's revaluation reserve before charging the balance to P&L. Several also capitalised the ₹10,800 delay-related expenses instead of expensing them, since the asset was already ready for use on 1st October, 2022.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Cost of a self-constructed asset - directly attributable costs only, excluding relocation/inauguration   +   Topic 4.4/4.9: Eligible borrowing cost net of temporary-investment income, capitalisation period
question_html:
On 1st April, 2024, Y Limited purchased an industrial plot of land for ₹50,00,000 for the purpose of constructing a new factory. This cost of ₹50,00,000 included legal cost of ₹2,50,000 incurred for the purpose of acquisition of this plot. The construction of the factory commenced on 1st May, 2024. Y Limited provides you with the following details of the costs incurred in relation to the above construction:

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Preparation and levelling of the land1,60,000
Employment costs of construction workers (per month)58,000
Purchase of Raw materials for the construction42,48,000
Cost of relocating the workers to new factory for work75,000
Costs of inaugural function of the new factory on 1st January, 202595,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (per month)50,000

The construction of the factory was completed on 31st December, 2024 and production could commence on 1st February, 2025. The overall useful life of the factory building was estimated at 40 years from the date of completion. However, it was estimated that the roof would need to be replaced 20 years after the date of completion. The cost of replacing the roof at current prices would be 25% of the total cost of the building. The construction of the factory was partly financed by a loan of ₹56,00,000 raised from State Bank of India on 1st April, 2024 at an interest rate of 9% per annum. During the period when the loan proceeds had been fully utilized to finance the construction, Y Limited earned an income of ₹50,000 from the temporary investment of the proceeds. Assume that all of the net finance cost needs to be allocated to the cost of factory (excluding land) and interest cost to be capitalized based on eight months' period.

You are required to compute the carrying amount (i.e. value after charging depreciation) of the Factory in the books of Y Limited as at 31 March, 2025 as per the provisions of the relevant Accounting Standard.
answer_html:
Cost of construction of the factory

Cost of Industrial Plot50,00,000
Preparation and levelling of the land1,60,000
Employment costs of construction workers (₹58,000 per month) for 8 months4,64,000
Purchase of Raw materials for the construction42,48,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (₹50,000 per month) for 8 months4,00,000
Interest on ₹56,00,000 for 9 months @ 9% = ₹3,78,000 less ₹50,0003,28,000
Total Cost (A)1,06,00,000
Depreciation (B) (W.N.)43,750
Carrying amount of the factory (A−B)1,05,56,250

Working Note: Calculation of Depreciation

On land of ₹50,00,000: Nil. On remaining cost of Building i.e. ₹1,06,00,000 − ₹50,00,000 = ₹56,00,000:

  • On Building: ₹56,00,000 × 75% / 40 yrs × 3/12 = ₹26,250
  • On roof: ₹56,00,000 × 25% / 20 yrs × 3/12 = ₹17,500
  • Total Depreciation charged = ₹43,750

Cost of relocating the workers to new factory for work and cost of inaugural function of the new factory is not directly attributable to construction cost, hence not considered.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees included the relocation cost and the inauguration-function cost in the capitalised cost of the factory, failing to apply AS 10's distinction between costs necessary to bring an asset to its working condition and costs merely associated with commissioning it. Several also capitalised the gross interest of ₹3,78,000 without netting the ₹50,000 temporary-investment income against it, as AS 16 requires.
